history.reframe: The grotto or the open onsen is my call. Metropolis sampling belongs where paths are hard to find, such as caustics from the water onto the vault.

history.title: A front for the cave, and a terrace below it
history.frame: I asked for floor-to-ceiling windows onto the ocean, a patio, and rooms that are more open or more intimate, designed the way an architect would.
dimensions: what each camera sees through the glass
how deep a usable outdoor room must be
the sequence from public to private
history.move: A bronze-framed glass front inside the cave lip with two sliding doors where the kitchen and lounge cameras look in, a corbelled terrace 3.1 m deep, and cedar alcove screens.
history.backtalk: The parked kitchen door's pull touched the dining table, so the glass line moved 6 cm out. Ordinary 4 % glass turned the cut-away view into sky by day, so the front became anti-reflective glass. The olive's leaves floated free of its branches until it grew twigs.
history.reframe: The terrace is waiting for a sunset hour in the routine.

history.title: Lights that keep the house's hours
history.frame: Keep the light well, and add light installations inside and out that come on at different times of day.
history.move: A terrace festoon, a fire bowl, a soffit wash, stair step lights and a pool light, each on its own schedule. The eight lamps now follow the routine, and the bedside lamp works as a dawn lamp.
history.backtalk: Line lights use the exact irradiance of a glowing segment, checked against brute-force integration on 40 random layouts. Bounding boxes keep the festoon off the cliff under the ledge, and by day one uniform skips the whole term.
history.reframe: The pool light is where the Metropolis experiment meets the house, because its caustics on the vault are the hard paths.

history.title: A coast you can walk up to
history.frame: With visitors walking around outside, the cliff, plants and waves had to hold up at 5 to 10 m.
history.move: A camera-following sun shadow on the coast snapped to whole texels, twelve normal-only sea ripples, close-range sandstone detail, and a replanted clifftop of sage scrub, iceplant, grass and Torrey pines that loads after the first frame.
history.backtalk: Diagonal stripes on the near water survived turning off the shadows and the mirror; they were the swells themselves, one plane wave per octave. The first planting was 90 % bare and its pines read as dead snags. Streaming the planting shrank the first model from 1.65 to 1.00 MB.
history.reframe: Up close the tide-pool rocks looked dry (wetted the same day in `570bd80c8`), and the pines need bark plates.

history.title: Two renderers, one minute
history.frame: I agreed to the Metropolis experiment. Show, on light the house actually has, when Markov chain Monte Carlo beats independent sampling and when it does not.
dimensions: the sun's size against a minute's budget
how much of a visitor's processor the page may use
history.move: A dependency-free renderer of a simplified onsen whose single path sampler is fed independent numbers (path tracing) or mutated ones (Kelemen's Metropolis), raced in module workers on its own page.
history.backtalk: After a minute path tracing was off by 984 % and Metropolis by 180 %. Metropolis's total brightness is itself a rare-event estimate, because the bootstrap usually holds no sun path. Lazily replayed small steps left a few-percent bias until unread coordinates were redrawn, and a slab shortcut created ghost water hits that tests now catch.
history.reframe: The engine is ready for the pool light's caustics, and for manifold-based mutations if the race should be won outright.

history.title: More kinds of plant, from photographs of the real bluffs
history.frame: I kept the first replanting but found one kind of shrub boring, and asked what the landscape actually looks like.
dimensions: which species grow on the bluffs
where each grows relative to the cliff edge
bytes for a lazily loaded planting
history.move: A second planting on its own random stream. Sagebrush and wild oats form the matrix, lemonade berry fills the slope, prickly pear, yucca and rust-red iceplant grow on the rim, daisies line the walks, and one trimmed Canary Island date palm stands by the doorway.
history.backtalk: The rust iceplant read as a dark tarp because every mat had been wound clockwise, so its normal pointed into the ground; rewound, the old mats brightened to real iceplant green. A rim mat had stretched over a 7 m drop, the first oats looked like confetti, and the first palm like a spider. `flora.glb` grew from 1.18 to 2.2 MB.
history.reframe: If the inland hill needs cover, sparse sagebrush and oats are the cheapest step.

open_problems.title: A spectral ocean
open_problems.why_hard: The Pacific is ten authored Gerstner components. A spectral FFT ocean would give realistic wave statistics, but WebGL2 has no compute shaders, so the transform needs several ping-pong passes, cascades to hide tiling, and a CPU sampler that agrees with it, because floating objects and arrival rays read the same wave heights.
candidate_moves: Prototype a 128² FFT height field on a separate page and compare it with the authored spectrum from the same camera.
Keep the authored components for CPU sampling and use the FFT only for normal detail, so contacts stay exact.

open_problems.title: Caustics on the onsen vault and floor
open_problems.why_hard: Light reaching the vault or the pool floor through rippled water is a chain of specular bounces that must end in a small sun or a small pool light. Next-event estimation cannot aim through the water, which is the case the light lab measured, and the house has no runtime ray tracer.
candidate_moves: Add the pool light to the lab scene and render its caustics on the vault.
Precompute a caustic pattern from the lab and project it in the onsen, animated by the solver's slopes.
Try manifold exploration or specular manifold sampling in the lab before anything reaches the house.

open_problems.title: The outside view on integrated GPUs
open_problems.why_hard: Outside, about 1,600 draws a frame go through four passes: the view, the shadow map, the opaque copy refraction needs, and the sea mirror. Most objects are interactive, animated, wind-swayed or skinned, so batching could save 3 draws. Every remaining saving changes pixels.
candidate_moves: A distant, non-refracting onsen material outside, which drops the opaque copy (about 400 draws).
Skip objects smaller than a pixel (about 180 draws).
Judge each with a matched A/B before shipping.

open_problems.title: Temporal antialiasing
open_problems.why_hard: Without per-object motion vectors, temporal antialiasing would trade a little shimmer for ghosting on the characters, animals, plants and waves, which move on almost every frame. 8× multisampling cost about 3 ms of GPU time for no visible gain.
candidate_moves: Motion vectors for skinned and wind-deformed meshes.
A still photo mode where a temporal filter can accumulate.

open_problems.title: One wind for the whole coast
open_problems.why_hard: The room plants, particles and steam share the curl field, but the clifftop planting sways on its own sine rule and its shadows see the rest shape. Unifying them means patching the planting's beauty and depth materials with the same field and response, without breaking the divergence guarantee or the shader cache keys the warmup relies on.
candidate_moves: Bind the clifftop materials to `coastalWind` with the damped response from `plant-motion.mjs`.
Give the planting a custom depth material that runs the same bend.

open_problems.title: Cloth that moves
open_problems.why_hard: The duvets are offline drapes and nothing in the scene is runtime cloth. A curtain in the breeze or a duvet that breathes needs a solver that stays stable within the frame budget, attached to animated bodies.
candidate_moves: Start from the colored Gauss–Seidel solver in `bin/coastal_bedding.py` and port a small extended position-based version to the browser for one curtain.
Drive it with the shared wind field.

open_problems.title: Light that sees people and plants
open_problems.why_hard: The traced light field is static and has one bounce, so the avatar, P and the swaying plants never shade it. Retracing on the CPU every frame is too slow, and probe updates in the style of DDGI rely on GPU ray tracing that WebGL does not offer.
candidate_moves: Subtract soft analytic occluders (capsules) for the avatar and P from probe visibility.

open_problems.title: Grotto or open onsen
open_problems.why_hard: The light well makes the bath a grotto that gets sun only through the shaft, so outside midday it is darker than the open cutaway was. Both are defensible; it is a taste decision.
candidate_moves: Keep the grotto.
Open the onsen and show the well only from the clifftop; `?onsen-light=open` previews it.

open_problems.title: A sunset hour on the terrace
open_problems.why_hard: The terrace has loungers, a bench and a fire bowl but no activity in the routine. A new activity needs fitted contacts, a camera that looks through a door opening, and a place in the schedule.
candidate_moves: Add an evening terrace activity with contacts on a lounger or the bench, timed with the festoon and fire bowl.

open_problems.title: Architectural and Illustrated treatments
open_problems.why_hard: In September the three treatments read as too similar, and Realistic worked best. A shader swap alone does not make a different way of seeing the same home.
candidate_moves: A same-camera comparison where each treatment has its own form, light, mark-making and motion, kept behind `?scene-lab=1`.

open_problems.title: Close-up character and environment detail
open_problems.why_hard: The scene is a stylized browser world. Film-studio character surfacing and close-up environmental detail remain a higher target, bounded by download size and frame budget.
candidate_moves: Pick one close-up (a face at the desk, the onsen rim) and compare a detail pass against the current frame at the same camera.
